transcript:
Header: 2026-11-04 10:00 PDT | Duration: 45 mins
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Sarah Cho (QuantaHealth Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Platform Eng), Priya Nair (SRE)

-- Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood and QuantaHealth review throughput tests. Main takeaways: 150ms batching window increased batching efficiency but pushed p99 above target for some tails; 50ms window with higher concurrency hit better p99 but lower batch efficiency; recommended intermediate window + concurrency cap + queue length limit.

00:00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check, is the audio ok?
00:00:03 Sarah: yeah good here, sorry running a little behind, got Priya and Tom on as well
00:00:10 Maya: awesome, quick agenda: go over the latest benchmark sheet Ethan ran, talk batching windows and conc limits, talk queueing/backpressure and next steps.
00:00:20 Ethan: i'll share my screen in a sec, but tl;dr we ran four configs across a 4-node A100 pool, quantized model to int8, tok/sec measures, and we toggled batching windows at 50ms, 150ms, 300ms.
00:00:35 Tom: when you say quantized, that's per your earlier recs, right—no custom kernels?
00:00:40 Ethan: yes, just standard RTX/amp + int8 path. Some kernels change, but nothing custom. We saw mixed results due to KV cache behavior.
00:00:48 Sarah: can you remind me of our target SLOs—i want to anchor numbers—p95 and p99?
00:00:52 Maya: target p95 < 120ms, p99 < 450ms ideally for the low-latency endpoints. Throughput target for the pilot was 600 rps burst, sustained ~300 rps.
00:01:06 Priya: right, and we care about tails because of downstream syncs, if p99 spikes we have cascading issues.
00:01:15 Ethan: ok slide 2 — results. With a 50ms batching window + concurrency cap 16 we hit ~320 rps sustained, p95 ~90ms, p99 ~320ms. Batching efficiency low — batch sizes avg 3.
00:01:33 Ethan: with 150ms window + no concurrency cap we got avg batch size 9, throughput ~520 rps, p95 ~140ms, p99 ~610ms — so tail hurt.
00:01:50 Tom: that 610ms p99 is concerning. Is that from queueing in the runtime or from model compute variance?
00:01:56 Ethan: mix of both. The larger batches grow decode time and amplify variance; also KV cache misses at cold keys increased decode time per token downstream. Our profiling shows a few outliers where cache not populated due to mid-session eviction.
00:02:12 Sarah: eviction—are you referring to the K-V cache, like the KV cache, right?
00:02:16 Ethan: yeah, sorry, K-V cash—i mean KV cache—transcription note, haha. When sessions are short and concurrency high we see more cold starts.
00:02:25 Maya: ok, so tradeoff is obvious — higher window gets more throughput, worse tails. Lower window better p99 but throughput suffers. We need a hybrid.
00:02:35 Ethan: proposed hybrid: 100ms batching window + concurrency cap 20, plus a queue length limit of 200 requests. Also enable prefix caching for common prompts (QuantaHealth has a common system prompt). In our sim that hits ~460 rps sustained, p95 ~110ms, p99 ~380ms.
00:02:52 Tom: 200 queue length, what's overload behavior? Do you drop or reject?
00:02:56 Ethan: runtime default is to queue up to the limit, then start returning 429s. We can also do adaptive shedding and prioritize low-latency endpoints, or route overflow to a cheaper model variant.
00:03:07 Priya: route overflow—are there privacy concerns with routing to hosted vs dedicated? we need to keep PHI in our VPC for compliance.
00:03:14 Maya: yes, we can keep primary traffic on private pool. Overflow routing would be within your dedicated pool tiers or to an isolated cheaper variant in the same VPC; we won't route outside unless you opt into hosted overflow.
00:03:26 Sarah: ok good. Back to numbers—how deterministic are these sim numbers vs real traffic?
00:03:30 Ethan: sims use traced inter-arrival times from a sample day Tom will provide. We still saw variance when we replay bursts. That's why we asked for a 30-minute representative traffic trace for next run.
00:03:42 Tom: i'll pull that, might need to scrub session ids before sharing.
00:03:46 Maya: that's fine, hashed ids are OK.
00:03:48 Ethan: another point—continuous batching has a tunable window and a concurrency cap. In some runs we hit the GPU occupancy sweet spot where 8-12 concurrent requests per GPU gave best latency/throughput mix. With 4-node pool (16 GPUs), cap=20 mapped well to overall concurrency.
00:04:06 Sarah: can you walk me through the math quickly? i want to know how you sized dedicated pool for 600 rps.
00:04:10 Ethan: sure, rough math: with our hybrid config, effective tokens/sec per GPU was ~3750 token/s; average tokens per request in your workload is ~80 tokens; that gives RPS per GPU ~46; with 16 GPUs that's ~736 rps headroom; we target 600 rps to keep buffer for burst. This matches the earlier A100 runs after quantization.
00:04:33 Tom: so that suggests 4 nodes of A100 is sufficient? any need for extra burst credits?
00:04:36 Maya: on Dedicated we recommend reserved pool sized to sustained needs plus burst credits for headroom. We'll size reserved for 300-350 sustained and allow burst to 600. We'll put numbers in the proposal.
00:04:47 Priya: what about prewarming and cache warmup—how long does it take to reach steady-state KV hit rate?
00:04:52 Ethan: depends on traffic. For your prompt shapes we saw KV hit rates climb to 85% after ~8-10 minutes of steady traffic for the default cache policy; with warmup hooks we can prepopulate important prefixes and get there in 1-2 minutes.
00:05:05 Sarah: warmup hooks—can we push a list of top 50 prefixes from our telemetry?
00:05:09 Ethan: absolutely, that will help reduce tails.
00:05:12 Tom: any changes needed on our side for connection pooling or client concurrency?
00:05:16 Ethan: recommend limiting client-side concurrency to avoid head-of-line blocking. Use a connection pool with max concurrency per worker ~8-12 and use adaptive retry/backoff. We can provide a client-side lib snippet.
00:05:29 Maya: ok, action items roundup in a bit. Quick question on observability—your console has token-level breakdowns right? can we get p99 per-route?
00:05:36 Ethan: yes, Redwood Console shows per-route p50/p95/p99 and token breakdowns, also per-model. We'll send a dashboard link and a short guide on setting alert thresholds.
00:05:46 Priya: for KMS rotation: do you support bring-your-own-HSM or just cloud KMS?
00:05:50 Maya: we support KMS integrations and can support HSM in Private deployment. We'll need to review your compliance checklist to confirm specifics.
00:05:58 Sarah: ok perfect.
00:06:00 Ethan: quick note on quantization—int8 gave a ~1.6x throughput improvement with minor quality delta; if you need further improvement we can explore gptq paths but that adds model onboarding time.
00:06:12 Sarah: let's hold off on gptq for now. We want to baseline on int8 first.
00:06:17 Tom: any anomalies in logs we need to be aware of? errors or OOMs?
00:06:21 Ethan: we saw a couple transient OOMs at 300 concurrency with 300ms window in one run—turned out memory fragmentation on older driver; re-run on updated driver cleared it. We'll record driver version in benchmark notes.
00:06:34 Maya: great. let's talk tuning plan — Ethan, you recommended a new run?
00:06:38 Ethan: yes, I'll run: 4-node A100, int8, configs: (50ms, cap16), (100ms cap20), (150ms cap25) with real traffic replay from Tom. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and batch sizes, kv hit rate, and GPU occupancy.
00:06:53 Maya: and include the warmup hook run where we prepopulate top 50 prefixes.
00:06:56 Ethan: yep.
00:06:58 Sarah: timeline ok? when can we expect the sheet?
00:07:00 Ethan: i'll share results and updated spreadsheet by Friday 2026-11-06.
00:07:05 Maya: perfect. next, quick ops question: what happens if queue fills and we start 429ing—do we want to retry client-side or fail fast?
00:07:12 Priya: from infra pov we prefer fail-fast for synchronous UX but implement a circuit-breaker for batches.
00:07:17 Tom: agree, fail-fast then fall back to cached response for non-critical flows.
00:07:20 Maya: good call. we'll document recommended retry/backoff semantics and sample code.
00:07:25 Sarah: on security checklist—still need SOC2 docs?
00:07:28 Maya: ye we shared SOC2 Type II, ISO and our audit log spec earlier; I'll attach the link in follow-up.
00:07:34 Ethan: final thing — routing policies: we can set policy to prefer low-latency model variant then fallback to cheaper variant when capacity hit; that helps cost. Tom: does that work with your compliance?
00:07:43 Tom: as long as both variants live in the same private environment or same VPC it's ok.
00:07:48 Priya: yep.
00:07:50 Maya: ok recap: Ethan runs the three benchmark configs + warmup run; Tom supplies traffic trace; Maya sends pricing + dedicated pool proposal; Priya confirms KMS/HSM requirements; everyone syncs on Friday if possible.
00:08:02 Sarah: sounds good. thanks all.
00:08:05 Maya: thanks team, will follow up with sheet + links.
